content: The classical definition of probability is closely associated with the work of Pierre-Simon Laplace. In his Théorie analytique des probabilités, Laplace articulated this definition as a direct consequence of the principle of indifference. According to this principle, if all elementary events are assigned equal probabilities, then the probability of a specific outcome (or a disjunction of outcomes) is calculated as the ratio of the number of favorable elementary events to the total number of possible elementary events. This definition assumes that all outcomes are equally likely. However, the classical definition of probability faced significant criticism during the 19th century. Prominent figures such as John Venn and George Boole questioned its validity. Their critiques, along with the influential work of R.A. Fisher, led to the widespread acceptance of the frequentist interpretation of probability. Despite this, the classical definition experienced a resurgence in interest due to the growing popularity of Bayesian probability. The mathematical study of probability emerged relatively late compared to other fields like geometry, even though evidence of humans engaging in games of chance, such as dice, dates back to prehistoric times. The formal birth of probability theory can be traced to the year 1654, when Blaise Pascal corresponded with Pierre de Fermat regarding two problems related to games of chance. These problems were introduced to Pascal by Chevalier de Méré earlier that year during a trip they took together. The first problem, known as the problem of points, dealt with determining a fair way to divide the stakes of a game that is interrupted before its conclusion. This problem had already been discussed by Luca Pacioli as early as 1494. The second problem involved a paradox related to extending a game of dice from one die to two dice. This paradox, discovered by de Méré, highlighted the potential pitfalls of applying mathematical reasoning to real-world scenarios. De Méré believed this paradox supported his philosophical view that mathematics, while elegant and precise, was often disconnected from the imperfections of reality and therefore of limited practical use. Pascal, a mathematician, was provoked by de Méré's philosophical stance and became determined to refute it by solving these problems using pure mathematics. He succeeded in doing so and later discovered that Fermat, an esteemed mathematician, had independently arrived at the same solutions using different methods. This mutual confirmation convinced Pascal that the problems had been definitively resolved. Their correspondence circulated among other scholars, sparking broader interest in mathematical problems arising from games of chance. It is important to note, however, that neither Pascal nor Fermat had a fully developed concept of probability at the time. For instance, they did not clearly distinguish between probabilities and expected values. The first individual to recognize the necessity of a precise definition of probability was Laplace. In 1814, he explicitly defined probability as follows: The theory of chance involves reducing all events of the same type to a finite number of equally possible cases—cases about which we are equally undecided regarding their occurrence. The probability of a specific event is determined by calculating the ratio of the number of favorable cases to the total number of possible cases. This probability is thus expressed as a fraction, where the numerator represents the number of favorable cases and the denominator represents the total number of possible cases. This statement by Laplace represents the classical interpretation of probability in its most explicit form.
